semantic.summary: Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature eco-lodge inside Ajloun Forest Reserve near Orjan, with wooden cabins and villas set in oak and pistachio woodland, a traditional restaurant and hiking trails.
semantic.description: Ajloun Forest Reserve is a protected woodland in the Ajloun highlands managed by the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature under its Wild Jordan brand, and the reserve operates its own accommodation inside the protected area. The lodging consists of wooden cabins arranged around a grassy clearing on the edge of the forest, with several tiers available: standard and deluxe cabins, a newer group of cabins named Pistachio, and a set of villas named Orchid. Listings describe a total of roughly thirty-eight cabins with a maximum capacity of about one hundred and forty guests per night, and the site operates year round. Each cabin has a private bathroom and a small private terrace facing the oak and strawberry-tree woodland that covers the reserve. A traditional restaurant on site serves local Jordanian dishes and can accommodate halal, vegetarian, vegan and gluten-free requests, and breakfast is served to staying guests. Shared facilities reported by guests and listings include a sun terrace, a lounge, a games room, a picnic and barbecue area, a gift shop selling products made by the reserve's local craft workshops, a tour desk for guided walks, and free parking. Marked hiking routes leave directly from the accommodation area, including the trails toward Orjan and Rasoun villages. Booking is handled through the Wild Jordan reservation system rather than through most conventional travel agents.

location.address: Arjaan (Orjan) Village, Ajloun Forest Reserve, Ajloun 26810, Jordan

context.notes: Operated by the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature under the Wild Jordan brand. Reservations are made through the Wild Jordan booking system. Hiking trails toward Orjan and Rasoun start from the accommodation area.

governance.source: Official Website (RSCN / Wild Jordan) + Booking.com Listing + TripAdvisor + Google Search

semantic.summary: Two-star, twenty-room hotel on Castle Street at Halawa Crossing in Ajloun, roughly two kilometres from Ajloun Castle, with air-conditioned rooms, a garden, a terrace, a bar and free parking.
semantic.description: Al-Jabal Castle Hotel is a small two-star property on Castle Street at the Halawa crossing in Ajloun, positioned on the road that climbs toward Ajloun Castle and set about two kilometres from both the castle and the town centre. Listings put the size of the property at around twenty rooms, including suites and family rooms alongside standard doubles. Rooms are air-conditioned and have private bathrooms with complimentary toiletries, a telephone, a safe and a wake-up service, and free wireless internet reaches the guest rooms and public areas. Shared spaces described across listings include a garden, an outdoor terrace, a shared lounge and a bar, and the hotel provides free breakfast, room service and daily housekeeping. Barbecue facilities are available for guests, and the hotel arranges airport transfers on request. The property is reported as pet-friendly on its listings, and free on-site parking is available. Because of the elevation on the Ajloun ridge, most rooms and the terrace look out over the wooded hills of the governorate. Guest scores across major platforms are moderate rather than high, and reviewers generally describe the property as a functional and inexpensive base for visiting Ajloun Castle and the surrounding forest rather than a full-service hotel. Typical nightly rates observed on booking platforms sat in the range of roughly fifty to sixty-five Jordanian dinars depending on season and room type.

location.address: Castle Street, Halawa Crossing, Ajloun 26824, Jordan

context.notes: Around 20 rooms. Approximately 2 km from Ajloun Castle and from the town centre. Barbecue facilities available to guests.

semantic.summary: Forty-room budget hotel on Al Rabadh Castle Street in Ajloun, a short drive below Ajloun Castle, with a swimming pool, a bar, a restaurant, laundry service and free parking.
semantic.description: Ajloun Hotel is a long-established budget property on Al Rabadh Castle Street, on the approach road to Ajloun Castle and a few minutes by car from the castle gate. Listings describe forty guest rooms across the building. Rooms are air-conditioned and include a refrigerator and minibar, a safe and a private bathroom, and free wireless internet is available. Because the hotel sits on the hillside below the castle, many rooms and terraces look out over the wooded valley, and reviewers consistently rate the location and the views as the property's strongest feature. Facilities described across listings include an outdoor swimming pool, a bar and lounge, a restaurant, a business centre, room service, dry cleaning and laundry service, luggage storage, a shuttle bus service and organised children's activities. A continental breakfast is served in the morning and is charged separately rather than included in the room rate. Free self-parking is available on site. Guest reviews are mixed: the setting and the outlook toward Ajloun Castle draw praise, while cleanliness and the condition of the rooms receive noticeably weaker scores, and several reviewers note that the position outside the town centre makes a car useful. Nightly rates observed on booking platforms were typically in the region of twenty-five to thirty Jordanian dinars, placing it at the lower end of the local market.

location.address: Al Rabadh Castle Street, Ajloun 26810, Jordan

context.notes: 40 guest rooms. Continental breakfast is served daily for an extra charge and is not included in the room rate. Reviews rate location highly but room condition and cleanliness poorly.

semantic.description: The Olive Branch Hotel is a three-star, family-run property set on a hill on Guzn Al-Zaytoon Road, reached from the Jerash to Ajloun road a short drive west of the Jerash ruins. The setting is rural, with olive groves around the buildings and an open outlook toward Dibeen Forest Reserve and the surrounding pine-covered hills. Listings and review sites describe a property of roughly thirty-three to fifty-five rooms across the main building and separate units, with non-smoking rooms, family rooms, garden rooms and mini apartments among the categories available. Rooms have air conditioning, a flat-screen television, a telephone, a wake-up service and a private bathroom, and free high-speed wireless internet reaches the whole property. Facilities include an outdoor swimming pool, the on-site Zaitoun restaurant serving international and traditional Jordanian dishes prepared with the family's own olive oil and warmed in winter by a wood-burning fireplace, a games room with table tennis, meeting rooms, barbecue facilities, a currency exchange desk, room service and a front desk staffed around the clock. Free parking is available on site. Check-in begins at 13:00 and check-out is until 12:00 according to published listings. The hotel is the highest-ranked conventional hotel in Jerash on major review platforms, and nightly rates typically observed sat in the region of forty to fifty Jordanian dinars.

semantic.summary: Small five-room family-run inn on Jerash Main Road directly opposite Hadrian's Arch, a few minutes on foot from the Jerash Visitor Centre, with a rooftop terrace and complimentary breakfast.
semantic.description: Hadrian's Gate Hotel is a small owner-run guesthouse on Jerash Main Road, positioned directly opposite Hadrian's Arch, the monumental gate raised at Gerasa around 129 AD to mark the emperor's visit. The location is as close to the archaeological site as any accommodation in the city: the Jerash Visitor Centre is roughly a five-minute walk away and the Jerash Archaeological Museum about six minutes on foot. The property is very small, with five guest rooms, and is classed on review platforms as a bed and breakfast or inn rather than a hotel. Rooms are described as having a refrigerator, a flat-screen television, pillowtop beds and cotton bed linen, with private bathrooms. A complimentary continental breakfast is served each morning, and the house also holds a daily manager's reception for guests. A rooftop terrace gives an open view across the main road toward the ruins. Wireless internet is available in the public areas, and the guesthouse offers express check-in and check-out along with concierge assistance for arranging site visits and onward transport. Free parking is available. The property ranks first among the small inns of Jerash on major review platforms, and reviewers repeatedly single out the hospitality of the owner and staff and the walking-distance proximity to the ruins as the reasons to stay. Published check-in and check-out times and cancellation terms were not confirmed.

Rooms are air-conditioned with private bathrooms, and family rooms are among the configurations offered; in-room provision described in listings includes a tea and coffee maker, a mini-bar, a television and free wireless internet, with city views from many rooms. Free private parking is available on site. The hotel's central position places it within a short walk of the Jerash ruins and of the town's established eating places, including Ya Hala Restaurant and Al Khayam Restaurant. semantic.summary: Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature eco-lodge in Azraq, converted from a 1940s British military field hospital, with sixteen air-conditioned rooms, a restaurant run by a local family and easy access to the eastern desert reserves.
semantic.description: Azraq Lodge is an eco-lodge in the oasis town of Azraq, in the eastern desert of Zarqa Governorate, operated by the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature under its Wild Jordan brand. The building was originally a British military field hospital dating from the 1940s and was restored and converted into visitor accommodation, keeping the period character of the structure. Listings describe sixteen fully equipped rooms in a 1940s style, air-conditioned, each with a private bathroom and a terrace looking out over the town and the sand flats of the surrounding basin. The rooms hold thirty-two beds as standard, and extra beds or mattresses can raise the maximum capacity to around thirty-eight guests per night. A restaurant and kitchen on site are managed by a local family and are known for home-cooked Chechen dishes, reflecting the mixed Bedouin, Chechen and Druze communities of the town from which the lodge draws its staff. A buffet breakfast is served to staying guests, with halal and vegetarian options available. Shared areas include a terrace, a garden and outdoor seating. The lodge is used mainly as a base for visiting the wetland and wildlife reserves of the eastern desert, and reservations are handled through the Wild Jordan booking system as well as through mainstream travel agents.

context.notes: Operated by the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature under the Wild Jordan brand. Sixteen rooms, standard capacity thirty-two beds. Guests are asked to inform the property of their arrival time in advance. The kitchen is run by a local family and serves Chechen home cooking.

semantic.description: Azraq Rest House is a three-star property in Al Azraq ash Shamali, the northern half of the Azraq oasis town in Zarqa Governorate. It is one of the older rest houses on the eastern desert route and sits close to the town centre, a few minutes by car from the black basalt desert castle. Listings describe a property of around fifty-eight rooms, including family rooms, each with a private bathroom, air conditioning and its own balcony, terrace or patio, with outlooks over either the garden or the pool. The grounds include a garden, a terrace, an outdoor dining area and a swimming pool with a view, along with a hot tub. A restaurant and a bar operate on site and room service is available. The property runs a 24-hour front desk, offers free private parking on site, and can arrange a paid airport transfer for guests arriving from Amman. Because of its position on the highway east toward the Iraqi and Saudi borders, the rest house is used both by tourists visiting the desert castles and wetland reserves and by travellers breaking a longer drive. Rates sit at the lower end of the Jordanian market, and reported check-in is early, from midday, with check-out the following morning.

A complimentary buffet breakfast is served each morning, and the hotel restaurant is open for lunch and dinner, with room service available during limited hours. Other services listed include free wireless internet throughout, free on-site parking, laundry service, a front desk and a non-smoking policy across the building. Reported check-in is from early afternoon with a midday to early afternoon check-out. The hotel is positioned for visits to the Azraq oasis area, with the black basalt fort a short drive away and the wetland reserve roughly ten minutes by car, and it also sits close to the Muwaffaq Salti air base. Directory listings for the property appear under both the Azraq area of Zarqa Governorate and neighbouring Mafraq Governorate, so the exact administrative placement should be confirmed before the record is used in itinerary planning.

It stands in the Batrawi district in the north of the city, close to the junction locally known as JK Circle, which puts it within easy reach of the city centre and of the highway link toward Amman. Listings describe a property of roughly forty-nine to fifty rooms and suites, all air-conditioned and equipped with minibars and flat-screen televisions. An on-site restaurant serves international cuisine and is open for breakfast, lunch and dinner, and breakfast is included in the room rate. Wireless internet and on-site parking are provided without charge, and the hotel runs a 24-hour front desk. An airport shuttle to and from Queen Alia International Airport is available around the clock for a fixed fee per vehicle each way. Reported check-in is from mid-afternoon with check-out at midday. Because Zarqa is primarily an industrial and commercial city rather than a leisure destination, the hotel's guests are largely business travellers, contractors and visitors to the surrounding governorate, and it also serves as a practical base for reaching the eastern desert sites of the governorate.

semantic.summary: Four-star forest lodge in the Zay countryside outside As-Salt, with ten imported timber chalets set among pine and oak, two swimming pools, an international restaurant and an activity park including paintball, archery and padel.
semantic.description: Mountain Breeze Lodge & Resort sits in the countryside of the Zay area of Al-Salt, in the Balqa highlands, with views over the surrounding Gilead mountains. The property has ten units, offered as one-bedroom chalets of about 36 square metres sleeping two, and two-bedroom chalets sleeping four. The lodges are imported prefabricated timber cabins built entirely of high-quality wood, each placed in its own section of the resort's pine and oak forest. Every unit is air conditioned and has a flat-screen television, a free mini-bar, a safe deposit box, coffee-making facilities, a seating area and a private balcony; bathrooms have a bath or shower plus bidet, with bathrobes and slippers provided. The resort operates two swimming pools, an adults-only pool with mountain views and a separate family pool. Dining is at an international restaurant with a bar, and there are several open-air terraces overlooking the gardens and forest. On-site activities are unusually extensive for a property of this size and include the Jordan Paintball Club, an archery range, padel courts, billiards, guided hiking trails, a children's playground, a tree house, a small animal village and bonfire nights. Free private parking is available and the property offers an airport shuttle service. Pets are not allowed and no cots or extra beds are available. It is ranked the top hotel in Al-Salt on major review sites, with guest scores around 8.8 across more than 190 reviews. The Aremeiman waterfall is about ten minutes away by car.

semantic.summary: Boutique hotel in a restored 1905 family house inside the UNESCO-listed historic core of As-Salt, with modern and original stone rooms, a Jordanian restaurant on a terrace over the old town, and community craft experiences.
semantic.description: Beit Aziz Boutique Hotel occupies a restored family house dating from 1905 in the UNESCO World Heritage core of As-Salt, and is widely described as the town's first boutique hotel. The building had stood vacant for more than twenty years before restoration, which was supported by external development funding because of the house's historic significance. It is owned and run by a Jordanian family rather than a chain. Accommodation is split across two wings: three modern, light-filled rooms with panoramic views over the town, and two original stone rooms with restored stonework and vaulted ceilings, with booking channels recording four bookable rooms. Rooms are air conditioned with minibars, complimentary bottled water and flat-screen televisions with satellite channels, and are made up with Egyptian cotton sheets. The on-site restaurant serves Jordanian dishes including sajiyeh, mansaf and fatteh using locally sourced ingredients, and its terrace looks out over downtown As-Salt. Guests can join craft-making and cooking experiences led by local women as part of a community-empowerment programme linked to a regional handicraft project. Interiors are furnished with traditional Jordanian pieces and the architecture shows Ottoman-era detailing in yellow sandstone, with arched windows and domed roofs. A 24-hour reception, room service, paid laundry and dry cleaning, a coffee shop and free parking are available. Sources conflict on whether breakfast is included, so guests should confirm at booking. The Salt Archaeological and Folklore Museum is about five minutes away on foot.

semantic.summary: Six-room heritage guesthouse in a century-old building on Al-Khader Street inside the UNESCO-listed core of As-Salt, themed around the traditional Jordanian madhafa guest space, with a free halal breakfast and city-view rooms.
semantic.description: Jordan Heritage Madhafa occupies a heritage building on Al-Khader Street inside the UNESCO World Heritage core of As-Salt, described in listings as being between one and two centuries old. A madhafa is the traditional Arabic guest space, and the property is explicitly themed around traditional Jordanian hospitality; it is operated in association with Jordan Heritage, the organisation behind the country's living-history and heritage revival programmes. The guesthouse has six individually decorated rooms, all air conditioned with private bathrooms; some rooms have a terrace and some look out over the town. Two categories are offered, a Classic Room with either two single beds or one king bed, and a Panoramic Room with a king bed and a city view. A free halal breakfast is served every morning in the restaurant, and there is a coffee shop and a garden. Free self-parking is offered on site, along with a cash machine, a convenience store and a first-aid kit, and free WiFi covers both the public areas and the guest rooms. Pets are not allowed, and service animals are also not accepted. Payment is taken by Visa, Mastercard or cash. Guest ratings sit around 8.5 across more than 320 reviews. The property is surrounded by heritage buildings and churches and is minutes from the town's traditional souqs, the shrine and church of Saint George on the same street, and the Salt Archaeological and Folklore Museum.

semantic.description: Al Hummar Restaurant & Hotel stands on Princess Tasneem Bint Ghazi Street in Fuheis, roughly seven and a half kilometres from the centre of Al-Salt. The establishment has around thirty years of operating history and is a well-known local institution rather than a modern build. Its architecture blends traditional and modern elements, with stone carving and ornate detailing, and historical photographs and artefacts are displayed throughout the property. The restaurant is the main draw, specialising in Lebanese and Mediterranean cuisine with mezze platters and grilled meats alongside Jordanian staples such as mansaf and maqlubeh. There are extensive indoor and outdoor seating areas with garden views, and the venue regularly hosts engagements, weddings and graduation events. Guest rooms are air conditioned with free WiFi, a refrigerator, a private bathroom and a balcony with mountain views, and the decor is simple with wooden furnishings. The hotel offers 24-hour room service, a fitness centre, a bar, a garden and terrace, and a tour desk for local excursions. Free valet parking is available, and car rental, dry cleaning, laundry and airport shuttle arrangements can be made on request. Pets are not allowed. It is effectively the only conventional bookable hotel property in the Fuheis and Mahis area, where accommodation is otherwise limited to private vacation rentals. One caveat: Fuheis sits close to the Balqa and Amman governorate boundary and booking channels index the property inconsistently between the two.

semantic.description: Mujib Chalets is a chalet village operated by the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature inside the Mujib Biosphere Reserve, on the Madash peninsula along the Dead Sea Highway in the Dhiban district of Madaba Governorate. The village opened in April 2008 and has fifteen en-suite double chalets built directly on the shore. Each chalet has an uninterrupted view over the water, a covered shaded terrace with hammocks, air conditioning and a private bathroom. The sea is about thirty metres from the chalets, with direct access to a rocky beach. Breakfast is included and served in a simple on-site restaurant, and dinner is available at extra cost. Free private parking is provided. The chalets sit about ten minutes' walk from the entrance to the Mujib Nature Reserve and adjacent to the Mujib Adventure Centre, and they function as the base for the Siq Trail and the Mujib canyon river hike, which are among the most popular guided wet-canyon routes in Jordan. The Society describes the location as offering some of the best views along the coast. The property operates seasonally in line with the reserve's hiking calendar, and reviews reference seasonal closures, though exact dates are not published, so booking directly with the Society is advisable. Amman is about eighty-six kilometres away and Ma'in Hot Springs about twenty-eight kilometres.

The property has 107 guest rooms and suites; rooms are air-conditioned and non-smoking, with flat-screen satellite television, minibar, electric kettle, wardrobe and a private bathroom with hairdryer and complimentary toiletries. Studio rooms with kitchenettes are offered for longer stays, and suite layouts include a separate living room and bedroom. Facilities described across the official website and listing sites include an indoor swimming pool, a jacuzzi, a sauna, a wellness and spa area, a fitness centre, and seven meeting rooms scaled for groups of roughly fifteen to four hundred people. The in-house Sevilla Restaurant serves international cuisine at breakfast, lunch and dinner. Check-in is from 14:00 and check-out is at 13:00. The combination of conference capacity, long-stay studios and a central Abdali-adjacent position makes the hotel a common choice for business and mixed-purpose travel.

semantic.description: Art Hotel Downtown stands at 30 King Faisal Street in Al-Balad, the historic core of Amman, surrounded by the souqs, coffee houses and street life of the old commercial centre. Listing sites record the property as a refurbished three-star hotel with 44 guest rooms; rooms are described as modern in finish, with a flat-screen television, a refrigerator and free wireless internet. The hotel's main draw is walkability to the city's principal archaeological sites: the Amman Citadel is roughly an eight-minute walk uphill, the Jordan Archaeological Museum on the Citadel grounds is about five minutes away, and the Roman Theatre is around a ten-minute walk. On-site services include a 24-hour reception, express check-in and check-out, an airport shuttle, luggage handling, a minimarket and an ATM. There is a patio and terrace with outdoor seating, and a lobby restaurant serving a family-oriented menu with vegetarian and halal options. Check-in begins at 14:00 and check-out is at 12:00. Because the hotel sits on a busy commercial street, quieter rooms tend to be on the higher floors. Baseline nightly rates recorded during research were in the region of 40 to 45 Jordanian dinars, placing the hotel in the mid-range band for central Amman.

semantic.summary: Long-established three-star boutique hotel on Mithqal Al Fayez Street in Jabal Amman's diplomatic quarter between the Third and Fourth Circles, with 38 garden-facing rooms, mature gardens, a terrace and a well-known bar.
semantic.description: Hisham Hotel is one of the older hotels in Amman, dating to the early 1960s, and occupies a low-rise property on Mithqal Al Fayez Street in Jabal Amman, in the embassy quarter between the Third and Fourth Circles off Zahran Street. The setting is unusual for a city hotel: the building is surrounded by mature gardens, with an outdoor dining terrace and a rooftop terrace, giving it a quieter and more residential character than the larger hotels on the main arteries. The hotel is non-smoking and has 38 air-conditioned rooms, most looking onto the garden, with some units including a lounge area or a private terrace. It is often described in boutique terms rather than as a standard three-star, reflecting the scale and the garden setting. The property is known locally for its long-running bar, generally cited as the oldest pub in Amman, and it also runs a cocktail and cigar lounge with music and sports broadcasts. An on-site restaurant serves Jordanian and Lebanese dishes, and a buffet breakfast is served each morning. Free wireless internet and free parking are provided. Check-in is from 13:00 and check-out is at 12:00. Rainbow Street and the First Circle area are a short ride away, and Downtown Amman is a further few minutes by car. Nightly rates recorded during research were typically around 45 Jordanian dinars.

semantic.description: Grand Mercure Petra stands on a hillside above Wadi Musa on Queen Rania Street, the road running south toward Taybeh, at an elevation of roughly 1,400 metres. The hotel traded as the Mövenpick Nabatean Castle Hotel until January 2024, when Accor rebranded it under the Grand Mercure name; the older name still appears on many distribution channels. It opened in 1995 and was built in a local Islamic architectural idiom, with crenellated stonework and massing that gives the building the outline of a castle. There are 90 individually decorated rooms and suites, each with a balcony, lanai or terrace and a complimentary minibar, and the rooms and suites were renovated in 2018. Facilities include an indoor swimming pool, a fitness centre, a restaurant, a bar and a coffee shop, with room service available around the clock, along with two meeting rooms and a business centre. The property holds Green Key and Green Globe environmental certification, and arranges horse riding and hiking. Its elevated position gives rooms an outlook over the Great Rift Valley and the Sharah mountain range. The Petra Visitor Centre is about a ten-minute drive downhill, so guests trade walking distance to the gate for the setting and the views.

semantic.description: Hayat Zaman Hotel & Resort Petra occupies the restored Ottoman-era village of Taybeh, roughly ten kilometres south of the Petra archaeological park. The village had been largely abandoned before it was conserved and converted into a resort, and the guest rooms are the original stone houses, reached along the narrow lanes and stepped alleys of the old settlement. Construction uses grand arches, vaults and local stone that keep the interiors cool in summer and warm in winter, and the restoration retained original materials and regional building style. The property traded for many years as Taybet Zaman Hotel & Resort, and that name persists in some booking channels. Rooms are air-conditioned with flat-screen satellite television, a fridge, a kettle and a private bathroom with a shower, and suites have central heating. The resort restaurant serves regional cuisine and opens onto a large sun terrace, and a buffet breakfast is included in the rate. Other facilities are an outdoor swimming pool with a poolside bar, a traditional Turkish bath and massage room, a fitness room, and billiards and table tennis rooms. Laundry and dry cleaning are available, and a private shuttle can be arranged to Petra, Wadi Rum and the coast. Rooms and terraces look out over the Sharah mountain range. Rooms are traditionally furnished and equipped with air conditioning, a minibar, a safe, an LCD television and tea and coffee facilities, and most look toward the surrounding mountains. The front desk and room service run around the clock, and a business centre offers translation and courier services. Parking is free and self-service. All rooms are air-conditioned and have private bathrooms with bathtubs and hairdryers, minibars, satellite television and a 24-hour movie channel, and they overlook either the Petra mountains or the hotel's pools. The hotel also operates a Turkish bath alongside a sauna, a steam room and paid massage services. It has 135 guestrooms, many with private balconies or patios, fitted with flat-screen televisions, safes, air conditioning and minibars stocked with complimentary items. Its restaurant serves international cuisine and part of the dining space is a cave room carved into the rock, which is the hotel's most distinctive feature. A complimentary buffet breakfast is served each morning. Wellness facilities include a traditional hammam, a sauna and a massage room. The hotel also provides a business centre, laundry and dry-cleaning, a tour desk and a barbecue and garden area. Accessibility is better documented here than at many neighbouring hotels, with a lift, handrails on the stairs, a stair-free main entrance and accessible rooms. Free valet parking is available on site, though advance reservation is required, and there is an electric vehicle charging point. A round-trip airport shuttle runs around the clock for a surcharge. The operator describes the hotel as a five-minute drive from the main gate of Petra, with the Petra Visitor Centre roughly two kilometres away in a straight line, so guests generally drive or take a taxi to the park rather than walking. Quoted nightly rates vary widely between distribution channels.

semantic.summary: Family-run Bedouin tent camp at Little Petra in Al Beidha, managed since 2010 by the local Mashaileh family, with six tent configurations, shared solar-heated shower blocks, an outdoor fire circle and breakfast included.
semantic.description: Seven Wonders Bedouin Camp lies at Little Petra in the village of Al Beidha, north of Wadi Musa, and has been family-owned and managed since 2010 by local Bedouins of the Mashaileh family. Accommodation is in tents rather than rooms, with six configurations covering double, twin, triple, family triple, quadruple and family quadruple layouts. Published rates run per tent per night depending on occupancy and include breakfast. Bathrooms are in two shared shower and toilet blocks supplied with hot water, so most tents do not have private facilities; towels are available on request. The camp provides beds, hot showers and wireless internet, and an outdoor fire circle where Bedouin tea is served and music is played in the evening. Meals include maqluba and kabsa with soups and salads, and breakfasts of hummus, olive oil and za'atar, eggs, jams, yoghurt, cucumber and tomatoes, olives and fresh flatbread; dinner is charged separately per adult and per child. Staff arrange hiking, four-wheel-drive trips and horse riding. Free parking sits beside the camp and the operator states that a four-wheel-drive vehicle is not needed to reach it. Little Petra and the Beidha Neolithic site are both close by. A separate and less rustic Seven Wonders Luxury Camp operates next door under the same family.

semantic.summary: Bedouin tent camp in Al Beidha run by the Salameen family, with air-conditioned standard and deluxe tents, a restaurant and café, and evening activities including henna, Bedouin coffee-making and arboud bread baking.
semantic.description: Little Petra Bedouin Camp occupies a site in the village of Al Beidha, close to the entrance of Little Petra and the Beidha Neolithic archaeological site. It is owned and operated by the Salameen family, a Bedouin family from Petra, and is positioned as an eco-oriented camp. Accommodation is in tents, listed in deluxe double, twin, triple and family configurations, the family tent having two single beds and one king bed. Standard tents are private but share bathroom and shower blocks, while a newer deluxe tent category has private bathrooms, so guests should check which category they are booking. Tents are described as air-conditioned, and free wireless internet and free parking are provided. On-site facilities include a restaurant, a café, a snack bar and a convenience store, and a buffet breakfast is served for a charge per adult rather than being included. The camp programmes evening and daytime activities including henna decoration, demonstrations of Bedouin coffee-making and the baking of arboud bread on an open fire, and it can arrange camel rides, jeep tours and guided hiking around Little Petra. Hundreds of small lights are lit among the rocks after dark. The front desk operates around the clock. Pets are accepted at no additional cost, though service animals are not permitted. Reported tent counts differ sharply between sources.

semantic.summary: Community-owned goat-hair tent camp in Wadi Al-Amti at Beidha, run by the Ammarin tribe through a cooperative of 200 families sharing revenue equally, deliberately offering no WiFi or air conditioning.
semantic.description: Ammarin Bedouin Camp lies in Wadi Al-Amti at Beidha, inside the Petra Archaeological Park and about ten kilometres north of Petra's main entrance, in a sandy enclave ringed by amphitheatre-shaped rock walls. The camp was established by the local Beidha community through the Beidha Tourist and Archaeological Cooperative and is run by the Bedouin Ammarin tribe; the owning cooperative is recorded as having 200 member families who share the revenue equally, making this one of the clearest community-tourism models in the Petra region. Guests sleep in traditional goat-hair tents with real beds and clean bedding, and the camp states a maximum capacity of 350 guests for camping and dining. Showers and toilets use hot water from a solar-thermal system, and towels can be rented. The camp deliberately provides no wireless internet and no air conditioning, though electricity for charging devices is available in the tents and the common tent. Communal meals are served in a traditional Beit Shar tent that is heated in winter, with dishes including mansaf, maqluba, kabsa and zarb. A paid shuttle runs from the Petra Visitor Centre or from Wadi Musa for up to four people. Activities offered with Ammarin guides include rababa making, carpet weaving, samer dancing, ten hiking routes and camel treks of up to four days.

semantic.summary: Domed-tent camp on the Wadi Nemelleh route in Al-Baydha, about 14 kilometres north of Petra, with three tent grades, private bathrooms, an outdoor pool, jacuzzi, sauna, fitness room and billiards room.
semantic.description: The Rock Camp Petra sits in the Al-Baydha area north of Little Petra, on the scenic Wadi Nemelleh route, and the operator places it about 14 kilometres north of the Petra archaeological site, a drive of roughly fifteen to twenty minutes. Accommodation is in domed tents across three named grades, from standard through superior to deluxe, and distribution listings map these to twin, triple and quadruple layouts plus a one-bedroom suite with a hot tub. Unlike the more traditional camps nearby, each tent here is furnished with beds, sheets, pillows and blankets and has satellite television, a mini-refrigerator and a private bathroom, which places the property closer to a resort than to a Bedouin camp. Facilities include an outdoor swimming pool, a jacuzzi, a sauna, a fitness room, a billiards room and gardens, along with a restaurant and a bar. Free parking, currency exchange and a laundry service for an extra charge are provided. Buffet breakfast is served in the morning and is charged separately per person. The main guest must be at least eighteen years old, and cots or extra beds cannot be added to tents. The operator publishes turn-by-turn driving directions from the Petra Visitor Centre and states that a standard vehicle is sufficient to reach the camp.

semantic.description: Petra Bubble Luxotel is a glamping property in the Al-Baydha and Little Petra area, north of Wadi Musa. Although it markets a Wadi Musa address, its mapped position falls administratively within the Shobak Qasabah District of Ma'an Governorate, and its published marketing distance to the Petra main gate is inconsistent with that position; the Petra Visitor Centre is considerably further than the advertised figure. The property consists of twenty bubble suites, each with a private bath, a sitting room and a bedroom under a transparent roof intended for night-sky viewing, and every bubble has its own jacuzzi and a terrace facing the Petra mountains and Little Petra. Room categories include king, twin, double and single bubble suites. An on-site restaurant with a stated capacity of 150 covers serves both western and eastern dishes, and a soft drink and a bottle of water are included with breakfast and dinner. Free wireless internet, a minibar, free private parking, conference facilities, a hair salon, a garden with a barbecue area and airport transfers are listed, along with a free shuttle to the main gate of Petra. The property operates as adults-only: the main guest must be at least eighteen and children are not permitted to stay. Pets are not allowed.

semantic.summary: Three-star social-enterprise hotel run by the Jordan Heritage Revival Company beside Shobak Castle, with 20 rooms with kitchenettes and balconies facing the valley, and live re-enactments of the Crusader–Saladin battle.
semantic.description: Montreal Hotel - Al Shobak stands beside Shobak Castle, the Crusader fortress known historically as Montreal, in the Shobak Qasabah District of Ma'an Governorate, roughly 700 metres from the castle itself. The hotel is operated by the Jordan Heritage Revival Company, established in 2010 under the King Abdullah II Fund for Development, which opened the property in 2016. It functions as a social enterprise: it employs military veterans who retire at the age of 36, provides them with health insurance and social security registration, draws staff from the local community across both the hotel and the castle, and makes regular local purchases. There are 20 individually furnished guestrooms with a stated capacity of 45 guests. Rooms have kitchenettes with refrigerators and microwaves, satellite television and balconies overlooking the valley toward the castle. Free wireless internet and free self parking are provided, along with a garden and a terrace. An on-site restaurant serves breakfast, lunch and dinner, and there is a coffee shop and room service around the clock. A business centre, laundry facilities and express check-out are available, and babysitting can be arranged for a surcharge. The hotel programmes live re-enactments of the twelfth-century battle between Crusaders and Saladin, along with castle tours, hiking, cycling and cooking classes.

semantic.summary: Twenty-six room solar-powered ecolodge at the south-western edge of the Dana Biosphere Reserve in Wadi Feynan, lit by candles after dark, reached by a 4x4 track and run as an all-inclusive stay with a vegetarian buffet and guided activities.
semantic.description: Feynan Ecolodge sits in Wadi Feynan at the south-western, desert edge of the Dana Biosphere Reserve, in Tafilah Governorate. The building is arranged as a candle-lit complex of courtyards, terraces and a roof used for stargazing and, in summer, for sleeping outdoors. There are 26 en-suite guestrooms in three grades: Economy rooms with single beds in twin, triple and family layouts; Standard rooms with twin beds or a king bed and an electric shower; and Deluxe rooms, which are larger and have private balconies. Lighting in the alcoves is by candle, showers are solar-heated and the small amount of electricity the lodge uses is solar-generated. Rooms have no power sockets, so devices are charged at the front desk, and complimentary limited WiFi reaches the lobby only. The stay is sold as a package covering the room, meals, guided activities, coffee, water and reserve entry; dinner is a vegetarian buffet and breakfast is Arabic. The last eight kilometres are unpaved, so guests without a high-clearance vehicle transfer from the Feynan reception centre near Qurayqira with a local Bedouin driver. Because of the lodge's remoteness, payment is normally cash only.

semantic.summary: RSCN-run guesthouse on the cliff edge at Dana Village with 24 rooms, private terraces over the wadi, an on-site reserve visitor centre and a function room, open year round and priced on a published tariff that includes breakfast and reserve entry.
semantic.description: Dana Guesthouse is operated by the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature and stands on the escarpment at the edge of Dana Village, looking down the wadi that the reserve's main hiking trails follow. It has 24 rooms in two grades: nine economy rooms that share one male and one female bathroom block, and 15 deluxe rooms with private bathrooms. All rooms open onto private terraces facing the mountains and the valley. The building also houses a small visitor centre with material on the reserve's geology, ecology and trails, together with a restaurant, a spacious terrace and a function room used for retreats, workshops and small conferences. Free WiFi is available in the public areas. Rates are published by RSCN on a fixed tariff with separate columns for Jordanians, residents and non-Jordanians, and include the reserve entrance fee, breakfast and a conservation fee. For non-Jordanians the 2025 tariff runs from JOD 70 for a single economy room to JOD 140 for a quadruple deluxe room. The guesthouse is open all year and its original capacity is 50 beds, with extra beds or mattresses available.

semantic.description: Rummana Campsite is the Royal Society for the Conservation of Nature's tented camp inside the Dana Biosphere Reserve, set on a hillside below Rummana Mountain with open views across the reserve. It holds 20 large tents and takes a maximum of 60 guests a night. Each tent is furnished with mattresses, blankets and pillows; toilets and showers are shared, towels are not provided, and there is no electricity anywhere on the site, so guests are advised to bring a torch. The camp and the hikes that start from it operate from 15 March to 31 October, with the dates subject to change if weather conditions require it, and the site closes for the winter. Published RSCN rates include the breakfast meal, the conservation fee and the shuttle service from the reserve entrance tower to the campsite and back, though unlike the guesthouse tariff they do not include the campsite entrance fee. For non-Jordanians the 2025 tariff runs from JOD 50 for a single tent to JOD 100 for a quadruple. The setting is dark, quiet and well suited to stargazing.

semantic.summary: Long-established budget hotel in the middle of Dana Village with about 20 individually themed rooms scattered across the building, a rooftop terrace used for sunsets and a nightly open buffet of home-cooked Jordanian food.
semantic.description: Dana Tower Hotel is one of the best-known budget addresses in Dana Village and is often described as the social centre of the village. Its roughly 20 rooms are spread across several levels and are individually decorated and named rather than numbered, with titles such as the Honeymoon Room, the Cave Room, the Sunset Royal and the Meditation Room. The rooms are simple, and several are unheated, which matters in winter at this altitude. The draw is the shared space: a rooftop terrace looking over the gorge that fills up at sunset, a restaurant that is open to non-residents, and an open buffet dinner of home-cooked Jordanian dishes that guests eat together, often followed by music. Breakfast is served as a buffet and is included in the tariff on most rates. The hotel has a 24-hour front desk, free WiFi in the public areas, a shared kitchen, a coffee corner, a safety deposit box and free parking, and it arranges hiking guides and onward transport. It suits independent travellers and hikers rather than guests looking for hotel-standard rooms.

semantic.summary: Community-run hotel occupying restored houses in the Ottoman core of Dana Village, opened by the local cooperative as the first hotel in Jordan run directly by a village community, with simple rooms and a nightly traditional dinner.
semantic.description: Dana Hotel was the first tourism venture of the Dana Cooperative and is described by its operators as the only hotel in Jordan run directly by the local community, with the income used to bring life back to the village. The rooms are restored houses belonging to families from Dana, spread through the fifteenth-century Ottoman village that is gradually being renovated, and the main entrance is in the centre of the village opposite the mosque. Double, triple, quadruple and family rooms are available, some en-suite and some with shared facilities. Rooms in the older part of the hotel were restored earlier and are plainer than the newer ones, and they are priced accordingly for guests on a tighter budget; guests report simple village-style rooms with en-suite bathrooms, feather duvets, a small kitchen corner and a heater for cold weather. Breakfast is included in the tariff and a traditional Bedouin dinner is cooked each evening. The roof is the gathering place, used for sunrise and sunset over the gorge. The hotel suits independent travellers who want communal meals and a village setting rather than hotel facilities.

semantic.description: This camp sits on the slope roughly a kilometre from the Ottoman village of Dana and near the start of the main wadi trail, looking out over the valley and the reserve. It is owned by a group of local farmers together with the village cooperative, and profits are returned to the community. Accommodation is mixed: four double rooms and two triple rooms, all en-suite, plus thirteen traditional tents sleeping one or two people that share shower and toilet blocks. Every unit faces the valley. The camp runs off-grid on solar power banks and spring water, and after dark it is lit by candles and lamps rather than mains lighting. Communal space is generous for a camp of this size, with a large Bedouin meeting tent, an indoor dining room with a panoramic window and an outdoor terrace. Breakfast is included in the tariff, while traditional lunches, dinners made from local ingredients and lunchboxes for hikers are bookable in advance. The on-site restaurant serves Middle Eastern food with vegetarian and halal options. Free WiFi and free parking are available, and guests are asked to contact the property in advance for check-in instructions.

semantic.summary: Bedouin-run eco camp on the cliff edge above the Dana canyon, several kilometres south of Dana Village, mixing traditional tents with stone houses that have private bathrooms, and using the camp as a trailhead for guided hikes into the gorge.
semantic.description: Al Nawatef Camp sits directly on the cliff edge overlooking the Dana canyon, a few kilometres south of Dana Village in Busayra District. It is run in Bedouin style and designed to sit lightly on the site: guests sleep either in traditional tents with proper beds and a small private terrace, or in stone houses that have their own bathrooms and toilets, with roughly 23 units in total across chalets and rooms. Meals are taken communally in the main Bedouin tent, and a traditional breakfast buffet is served each morning. Solar panels supply the showers and other basic needs. The camp is best known for its position and for the walking that starts from it, with several trails leading from the rim down into the gorge, and staff arrange guided hikes and horse riding. Other facilities include a restaurant, a snack bar, room service, a shared kitchen, a barbecue area, a garden, a playground, laundry service, a tour desk, free WiFi and free public parking. Pets are accepted on request at no charge, children aged six and under stay free without an extra bed, and the lead guest must be at least 18.

semantic.summary: Small owner-run hotel on the main street of Dana Village with double and triple rooms, a garden, shared lounge and terrace, a 24-hour front desk and a programme of guided hikes, village cooking sessions and Arabic lessons.
semantic.description: Dana Moon Hotel occupies a building on the main street of Dana Village, a short walk from the escarpment and the start of the reserve trails. It is a small property built around double and triple rooms, each with its own carpet and a fully equipped bathroom with a shower, and with tiled and carpeted floors throughout. Shared facilities include a garden, a lounge, a terrace and a guest kitchen, and there is free WiFi throughout the building and free private parking. The front desk is staffed around the clock and the hotel arranges airport transport. Breakfast is included in the tariff. What distinguishes the property is the activity programme run by the owners rather than the rooms themselves: guided day hikes in the reserve, multi-day walking routes, sessions learning to cook the village's food, time spent with Bedouin families and Arabic lessons with a local teacher. It is a practical, inexpensive base for walkers who want the village on their doorstep, and it works equally for solo travellers and small groups.

semantic.summary: Three-room heritage lodge in the old stone core of Dana Village, created by the owning family from their grandfather's house, with air-conditioned rooms, private bathrooms, balconies or patios and a small restaurant serving local cooking.
semantic.description: My Grandfathers House is exactly what the name suggests: the family home of the owner's grandfather in the old stone village of Dana, renovated and reopened as a small heritage lodge. The property is built from the original stonework and holds three well-appointed rooms, each air-conditioned, with a private bathroom and a balcony, terrace or patio looking onto the garden or the mountains. Family rooms are available and the scale of the place means service is personal rather than systematic; the family's hospitality is what guests most often single out. A halal breakfast is served daily and the small restaurant serves local cooking, with dietary variations prepared on request. Practical services are more extensive than the size suggests, including a tour desk, airport transfers, room service and a garden, shared lounge and terrace, along with free private parking and free WiFi. Hiking and horse riding are arranged nearby, and the reserve trails begin a few minutes' walk away. The lodge suits couples, families and travellers who would rather stay inside the historic village fabric than in a modern building on its edge.

semantic.summary: Village hotel at the upper edge of Dana with rooms that have seating areas and private bathrooms, several facing the mountains, plus a garden, shared lounge, terrace and a restaurant serving Jordanian and international dishes with reserve views.
semantic.description: Dana Horizon Hotel stands at the upper end of Dana Village, a few hundred metres from the old stone core and the escarpment where the reserve trails begin. Rooms are straightforward and comfortable rather than elaborate: each has a seating area, and the units have private bathrooms fitted with a bidet and free toiletries, with a number of them facing the mountains. Shared space includes a garden, a lounge and a terrace, and free private parking is available on site. Breakfast is served as a buffet with halal options, and the hotel's own restaurant is one of its stronger points, offering a menu that mixes traditional Jordanian dishes built on local ingredients with international choices, eaten within sight of the reserve. Guest feedback consistently picks out the hospitality, the food and the outlook rather than the fittings. The hotel is a reasonable middle option in Dana for travellers who want a private bathroom, a proper dining room and parking on site, without the price of the reserve guesthouse or the shared-facility simplicity of the village camps.

semantic.summary: Sixteen-unit hotel on the ridge above Dana Village at around 1,600 metres, marketed by its operator as the highest hotel in Jordan, with private entrances, an outdoor fireplace, a sun terrace and wide mountain views.
semantic.description: Jabal Dana Hotel occupies the top of the mountain ridge that encircles Dana Village, at an altitude the operator gives as about 1,600 metres and on which it bases its claim to be the highest hotel in Jordan. The property has sixteen units, each with outdoor furniture, a private bathroom with a walk-in shower and, in several cases, a private entrance; family rooms are available. The setting is the point of the place: a sun terrace, a garden, a patio and an outdoor fireplace all face the surrounding mountains, and there is a picnic area with barbecue facilities. A daily breakfast is served with a choice that includes vegetarian and halal options. Services include private check-in and check-out, a tour desk, a paid shuttle, free private parking on site and bicycle parking, with free WiFi throughout. Being on the ridge rather than in the village means a short drive down to the village trailheads, which suits guests arriving by car and less so those without transport. Payment is accepted in cash only.

semantic.summary: Locally run eco camp about ten minutes on foot from the reserve entrance, offering tents alongside double, twin, triple and family rooms with private bathrooms, and organising guided hikes, horse riding and night walks with a Bedouin team.
semantic.description: Dana Nabil Ecu Camp House stands near the main gate of the Dana reserve, roughly a ten-minute walk from the entrance and above the village itself. It is run as a cooperative venture: the operators describe the property as owned by around 120 local residents living within the reserve, with the proceeds directed towards food support for local families. Accommodation covers a wider range than the name suggests, with tents alongside double, twin, triple and family rooms, all of them with private bathrooms, and some units have a terrace. Free private parking and free WiFi are provided, and breakfast is served daily. Guests eat local cooking prepared on site. The activity programme is the property's main offer and is run by a Bedouin team: guided hikes ranging from two hours to full-day treks across the reserve, horse riding and night walks. Its position at the top of the approach road makes it a practical stop for guests arriving late or leaving early who do not want to descend into the village, while still being within walking distance of the reserve gate.

semantic.description: Dana's Trail Hotel is one of the larger conventional hotels in the Dana area, built around 30 smoke-free rooms rather than the handful typical of the village guesthouses. semantic.description: Alfares Hotel sits on the new highway on the approach to At-Tafilah, in the Al-Ays area of Tafilah Qasabah District, and is the main three-star address in the governorate's administrative centre. It is a conventional hotel rather than a village guesthouse: rooms are air-conditioned and come with a closet, an electric kettle, a safety deposit box, a flat-screen television, a balcony and a private bathroom with a bidet, and family rooms are available. The building has a restaurant, a garden and a terrace, and free private parking is provided on site without needing to be reserved. Pets are accepted on request, with any charge paid directly to the hotel. The position suits drivers heading between the King's Highway and the Dead Sea road, and the hotel functions as a practical base for visiting the Tafilah highlands and, at a distance of some twenty kilometres, the northern approaches to the Dana reserve.

semantic.summary: Eleven-room heritage property built into a historic stone village outside At-Tafilah, with self-catering rooms, fireplaces in some units, a restaurant, kids' club, garden, sun terrace, barbecue facilities and free bicycle hire.
semantic.description: Tafileh-Sila'a Heritage Village is a restored stone settlement turned into accommodation, set about seven kilometres from the centre of At-Tafilah among narrow alleys and stone houses with mountain views on all sides. There are eleven rooms. Several include a sitting area and a dining area, and selected units have a kitchen with a fridge, giving the property a self-catering character unusual in the governorate; all rooms have a kettle and a private bathroom with a bidet and free toiletries, air conditioning is fitted in some rooms and a number of units have a fireplace. Family rooms are available. Shared facilities include a restaurant, a kids' club, a garden, a sun terrace, barbecue facilities, luggage storage, free bicycle hire and free on-site private parking, and both a 24-hour front desk and room service are provided. Free WiFi covers the property. The rock-cut archaeological site at Sela is about a ten-minute drive away, and the northern edge of the Dana reserve lies roughly twenty kilometres off, which makes the village a workable base for exploring the Tafilah highlands rather than only a place to sleep between drives.
